questions.q: Why does a well-written prose runbook often still fail during a real 3 A.M. incident?
options: Prose runbooks are always factually incorrect
Under real pressure, responders scan for the next command instead of reading paragraphs, so the explanation gets skipped and they improvise from memory
Prose runbooks cannot be stored in version control
Paging tools are unable to display more than one paragraph of text
questions.explain: At 3 A.M. mid-incident, responders scan for the next action rather than reading explanatory prose, so a runbook written as narrative gets skipped rather than followed.

questions.q: Put the four sections of a 3 A.M.-ready runbook in the order this lesson recommends.
options: Escalate, Branch, Diagnose, Trigger
Branch, Trigger, Escalate, Diagnose
Trigger, Diagnose, Branch, Escalate
Diagnose, Escalate, Trigger, Branch
questions.explain: A usable runbook states the Trigger first so the responder confirms they're in the right doc, then Diagnose, then explicit Branch logic, then a clear Escalate condition.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist that runbook commands be fully concrete rather than templated with placeholders?
options: Mentally filling in a placeholder correctly is an extra cognitive step that's more likely to go wrong when a responder is half-awake under pressure
Templated commands run slower than concrete ones
Placeholders are not supported by most terminal emulators
Concrete commands are required by most paging tools' formatting rules
questions.explain: Filling in a blank correctly under pressure is exactly the kind of small step that goes wrong at 3 A.M.; a literal, exact command with real resource names removes that risk.

questions.q: What two triggers does the lesson give for when a runbook should be re-tested?
options: Only when a new engineer joins the team, and only once per year regardless of usage
Only during annual compliance audits
Only when the service's uptime drops below its SLO
Every time it's actually used in a real incident (validated during postmortem follow-up), and on a scheduled cadence via game days
questions.explain: Real incident usage should trigger a postmortem follow-up validation of the runbook, and independent of real incidents, scheduled game days exercise runbooks before they go stale.

questions.q: In the lesson's example runbook for high p99 latency, what determines whether the responder should manually scale versus follow a separate database-latency runbook?
options: Whether the alert fired during business hours or after hours
Whether any pod is over the CPU threshold and HPA replicas are at or below max, versus no pod being over threshold at all
Whether the primary or secondary on-call engineer is handling the page
Whether the service has passed its most recent Operational Readiness Review
questions.explain: The branch logic checks pod CPU against the HPA's current and max replica counts; if no pod is over threshold at all, the latency source is downstream and the engineer follows the separate db-latency runbook instead.
